items.title: Recap: Autonomy dominates the US Army’s 2026 conference in Washington
items.originalTitle: Recap: Autonomy dominates the US Army’s 2026 conference in Washington
items.summary: WASHINGTON — The Association of the United States Army showcased its annual conference from Oct. 12-14 in Washington, assembling defense industry officials, lawmakers and military personnel from around the globe to assess the future force and evolving threats. Army officials attending the conference emphasized the service’s need for rapid transformation as the technologies at the core of these conflicts seemingly evolve by the day. Defense News and Army Times covered these discussions — and more — from this year’s show.

items.title: New human-machine interface will help Boxer punch above its weight
items.originalTitle: New human-machine interface will help Boxer punch above its weight
items.summary: Sydney-based Breaker Industries, founded three years ago, is working with Rheinmetall Defence Australia to perfect the Avalon human-machine interface that will make a Boxer commander’s duties less onerous in the heat of combat. The two firms signed a teaming agreement on Oct. 6, the opening day of the Land Forces 2026 exhibition in Perth. Work will now continue for twelve months to mature the Avalon system for the Boxer, including trials slated for mid-2027.

With uncrewed systems proliferating on battlefields, Irwin said, “The goal is to allow an armored vehicle crew to easily work with teams of those autonomous systems like they were working with another crew member.” Indeed, he described the software stack as simply a “digital crew member.” Instead of having several extra soldiers dedicated to drone operation taking up space in the rear of the Boxer, this software helps the commander marshal all the assets in the proverbial toolbox.
The two firms signed a teaming agreement on Oct. 6, the opening day of the Land Forces 2026 exhibition in Perth.

items.title: Innovations sought for US Army’s electromagnetic spectrum effort
items.originalTitle: Innovations sought for US Army’s electromagnetic spectrum effort
items.summary: The US Army is conducting an Accelerated Capability Event (ACE) to evaluate, demonstrate and acquire operationally mature electromagnetic spectrum operations capabilities including in a counter-drone scenario. The Army is seeking innovative capabilities that demonstrate performance in a number of capability areas, including passive sensing solutions that detect, characterise and geolocate complex emitters without producing detectable RF signatures or overloading tactical networks.

evidenceRecords.text: The US Army is conducting an Accelerated Capability Event (ACE) to evaluate, demonstrate and acquire operationally mature electromagnetic spectrum operations capabilities including in a counter-drone scenario.

The Army is seeking innovative capabilities that demonstrate performance in a number of capability areas, including passive sensing solutions that detect, characterise and geolocate complex emitters without producing detectable RF signatures or overloading tactical networks.

The ACE effort enables US Army forces operating within a NATO and joint coalition framework on the Eastern Flank to sense, understand, exploit, attack and protect across a contested electromagnetic environment and connected cyberspace.
Selected vendors will receive prize funds and demonstrate their systems in Germany before Army and NATO end-users.
Winners will be onboarded into the US Army’s Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate (G-TEAD) Library of Competed Capabilities for potential follow-on procurement following the planned event.

items.originalTitle: Fast-flying Shahed drones spur new class of interceptors
items.summary: WASHINGTON\u2014A surge in Russia\u2019s use of jet-powered Shahed drones in Ukraine has spurred the need for super fast interceptors to defeat them. And it\u2019s a problem U.S.-based dronemaker Powerus hopes to solve.\u00a0 \u201cWe constantly need to move ahead of the threat. “We constantly need to move ahead of the threat.
The next threat that we see to get in front of is the jet-powered Shahed drones,” Brett Velicovich, cofounder and president of the dronemaker Powerus, told Defense One .
“Jet-powered Shaheds are very difficult to defeat because of how fast they are, and so to defeat those, we need jet-powered interceptors.

There's a good chance that by the end of this year, the majority of Russian drones that are sent into downtown Kyiv will be jet-powered,” he said, “so we really need to move at that timeline.” But churning out rocket- or jet-propelled interceptors at the same rate as the upgraded Shahed drones can be costly and difficult.

Newer versions of Shahed drones propelled by jet engines have increasingly been appearing on the Russian-Ukrainian battlefield in recent months, pushing Ukraine to fortify its air defenses.

Other versions of the Shahed fly just over 100 mph.

items.title: Lockheed invests $300M in Texas plant to feed missile surge
items.originalTitle: Lockheed invests $300M in Texas plant to feed missile surge
items.summary: Lockheed Martin is investing $300 million to expand its plant in Grand Prairie, Texas, which supports all programs across its Missiles and Fire Control business, including the PAC-3 MSE and THAAD interceptors, the Precision Strike Missile and the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile. The company said Oct. 14 that the expansion will help the plant reach record production levels and deliver components to final-assembly sites, including Camden, Arkansas and Troy, Alabama. Nearly 800 production employees work at the plant, which produced 250,000 parts in 2025.

evidenceRecords.text: Lockheed Martin is investing $300 million to expand its plant in Grand Prairie, Texas, which supports all programs across its Missiles and Fire Control business, including the PAC-3 MSE and THAAD interceptors, the Precision Strike Missile and the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile.
The company said Oct. 14 that the expansion will help the plant reach record production levels and deliver components to final-assembly sites, including Camden, Arkansas and Troy, Alabama.
Nearly 800 production employees work at the plant, which produced 250,000 parts in 2025.
Lockheed said it has added more than 30 high-precision machines in recent months and expects to install nearly 100 additional machines by the end of 2026.
Lockheed also said Hadrian, a California-based manufacturing startup, will install 24 automated machines at the Grand Prairie facility to produce missile parts.
Lockheed employees will operate the equipment, which is expected to be up and running by early 2027.
The project follows a memorandum of understanding the two companies signed in December 2025.
The buildout supports a series of framework agreements the Defense Department has signed with Lockheed since January, designed to boost missile production and lead to long-term contracts.
The first aims to increase PAC-3 MSE production from about 600 to roughly 2,000 interceptors per year over seven years.
A separate THAAD framework, signed in January, led to a June contract from the Missile Defense Agency worth more than $35 billion to quadruple interceptor production.
Lockheed and the Pentagon announced similar agreements for the Precision Strike Missile on March 25 and for the AIM-260 on Sept. 17.

“Lockheed Martin has brought together commercial speed and combat-proven performance because America needs both,” said Jim Taiclet, Lockheed’s chairman, president and CEO. “By combining advanced technology with the expertise of our American workforce, we’re transforming manufacturing to deliver critical munitions at speed and scale.”

items.summary: Less than one year after contract award, Saab, the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration (FMV) and the Swedish Armed Forces have successfully developed, built and launched a demonstrator for a Large Uncrewed Underwater Vehicle (LUUV). Developed at pace and according to plan, the demonstrator has progressed from concept to a fully functional vehicle. Following successful sea trials, the first phase of the project has been completed. The next phase is expected to focus on developing more advanced capabilities.

evidenceRecords.text: Less than one year after contract award, Saab, the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration (FMV) and the Swedish Armed Forces have successfully developed, built and launched a demonstrator for a Large Uncrewed Underwater Vehicle (LUUV).
Saab press release Developed at pace and according to plan, the demonstrator has progressed from concept to a fully functional vehicle.

The fact that we have also been able to develop and test the system in such a short timeframe demonstrates the strength of the collaboration between the Swedish Armed Forces, FMV and Saab,” says Mats Wicksell, head of Saab’s business area Naval.
The LUUV project builds on Saab’s earlier investments and work in autonomous underwater systems and is now led by FMV in cooperation with the Swedish Armed Forces and Saab.
Developed at pace and according to plan, the demonstrator has progressed from concept to a fully functional vehicle.
Following successful sea trials, the first phase of the project has been completed.
The next phase is expected to focus on developing more advanced capabilities.
The results will support the continued development of software, sensors and autonomous functions, while also contributing to future product development.
The vehicle illustrates how close collaboration between industry and government authorities can significantly reduce the time from identifying an operational need to testing a new capability.
“This project demonstrates how new technologies can be rapidly translated into practical operational value.
The uncrewed underwater vehicle can contribute to increased endurance, enhanced situational awareness and strengthened underwater capabilities.
The demonstrator has been developed to support the development and evaluation of future underwater capabilities and to enable operations alongside existing naval platforms, such as submarines.

The rapid development has been enabled by Saab’s software-centric approach and the integration of Autonomous Ocean Core, Saab’s autonomous control system that provides surface and subsurface vehicles with autonomous capabilities.
Combined with Swedish expertise in submarine design and sensor integration, this has made it possible to take the project swiftly from concept to sea trials.

items.title: France to go it alone on next-gen combat aircraft after FCAS collapse
items.originalTitle: France to go it alone on next-gen combat aircraft after FCAS collapse
items.summary: PARIS — France will develop a next-generation combat aircraft domestically as a successor to the Rafale, after a joint project with Germany and Spain for a future combat air system collapsed earlier this year, Air and Space Force Chief of Staff Jérôme Bellanger said. The country now conceives the future fighter, dubbed Avion de Combat du Futur or ACF, as a national project, with a target of flying conventional missions in 2040, Bellanger told the National Assembly’s defense committee in a hearing here on Wednesday.

evidenceRecords.text: PARIS — France will develop a next-generation combat aircraft domestically as a successor to the Rafale, after a joint project with Germany and Spain for a future combat air system collapsed earlier this year, Air and Space Force Chief of Staff Jérôme Bellanger said.

The country now conceives the future fighter, dubbed Avion de Combat du Futur or ACF, as a national project, with a target of flying conventional missions in 2040, Bellanger told the National Assembly’s defense committee in a hearing here on Wednesday.
“We’re now moving on to work that will prefigure and enable the birth of this ACF, this future combat aircraft as a national program,” Bellanger said.

France remains open to possible cooperation with other countries, “but within different frameworks and which won’t be structural to the birth of this aircraft.” France and Germany agreed to scrap the FCAS project in June, after years of wrangling about specifications and industrial control between Dassault Aviation and Airbus.

That’s left both countries without a clear successor for their existing fleets of Rafale and Eurofighter jets, respectively, though Germany has started receiving the first F-35 jets ordered in 2022 to replace the Panavia Tornado.

Dassault Aviation CEO Éric Trappier has said his company and France have all the know-how and skills to develop a next-generation fighter jet, together with engine partner Safran and defense-electronics firm Thales, and he would be able to do so “well below” a budget of €50 billion (US$56 billion).
All the years working on FCAS “haven’t been wasted,” with progress in areas including the aircraft, drones, stealth, connectivity and combat cloud, Bellanger said.
Work had been split up in several so-called pillars that also included a new engine, with Dassault and Airbus working on the next-gen fighter pillar at the heart of the system.
“The halt of the FCAS program doesn’t mean we’re throwing everything away,” Bellanger said.
“Our teams, the industrial teams have been working on the NGF, stealth, the cloud, and so on.

France will need to have a Rafale F5 standard in 2035 that incorporates the first components of the future combat aircraft, related to the engine, the sensors and the Stratus RS missile to neutralize enemy air defenses, according to Bellanger.

In September, Stoyanov said the NATO C-UAS initiative would stretch the Bulgarian defence budget and that it would duplicate efforts already underway in a European Union project.

However, following a series of maritime strikes in early October, in which two ships have been attacked by drones while sailing in the Black Sea, one of which was close to the Bulgarian coast, Stoyanov has said the defence ministry can find the funds to contribute and told parliament that it plans to join the C-UAS initiative by the end of the month.
He has also formally asked NATO to deploy C-UAS systems.

As the seventh and final unit to be delivered under the Programme, PPA 9 represents the culmination of a significant naval procurement initiative, providing the Italian Navy with a highly capable, flexible and technologically advanced platform designed to meet current and future operational requirements. – End –

On October 15, 2026, the First Steel Cutting Ceremony for the ninth Multipurpose Patrol Ship (PPA 9) was held at Fincantieri’s integrated shipyard in Riva Trigoso, officially marking the commencement of construction of the vessel and a significant milestone for the Programme.
The event marked the first physical stage in the construction process and underscored the continued cooperation between all Programme stakeholders.
Following Contract Amendment No. 10, PPA 9 will be constructed in the Full Combat Configuration, the most advanced and capable variant of the class.

items.title: ‘Revolutionary’: Bell touts MV-75 Cheyenne II as combat game changer
items.originalTitle: ‘Revolutionary’: Bell touts MV-75 Cheyenne II as combat game changer
items.summary: The U.S. Army’s MV-75 Cheyenne II is expected to bring increased capability to the service, not just through its boosted speed and range but also with its “digital backbone.” Although the Cheyenne being equipped with over double the speed and range of current weapons systems will be transformative, Bell, the defense manufacturer for the aircraft, anticipates the real “revolutionary” part to be its software, Frank Lazzara, Bell’s director of MV-75 Sales & Strategy, told Military Times in an interview.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Army’s MV-75 Cheyenne II is expected to bring increased capability to the service, not just through its boosted speed and range but also with its “digital backbone.” Although the Cheyenne being equipped with over double the speed and range of current weapons systems will be transformative, Bell, the defense manufacturer for the aircraft, anticipates the real “revolutionary” part to be its software, Frank Lazzara, Bell’s director of MV-75 Sales & Strategy, told Military Times in an interview.

The Cheyenne program is the service’s inaugural “digital-first” weapons system with a modular open systems approach , or MOSA, that allows the Army to virtually refine its architecture and helps acquire intellectual property and data rights needed to control future upgrades and avoid vendor lock-in.

“The Army is trying to set the standard for the government to have control over their maintenance, their upgradeability, like they’ve never had before,” Lazzara said at the 2026 Association of the United States Army conference in Washington, D.C.

Bell’s open system approach differs from others, he said, because it is guided and directed by the Army, giving them more control and changing the way business is conducted throughout the lifecycle of the aircraft.
“This is the model for what the government should get when they acquire a weapon system of this level and an acquisition at this level,” Lazzara said.

“That’s what gets lost out there.” “You can hang another system on an old aircraft, and you might have a little bit more capability, but you’re never going to have the capability you have in this aircraft, plus the ability to much more easily upgrade and maintain your aircraft through its life cycle,” he continued.

“That’s where the payoff really happens.” The Cheyenne , which is designed to be a multi-mission aircraft, is the Army’s next-generation tiltrotor assault and utility aircraft, slated to replace part of the force’s UH-60 Black Hawk fleet.

Yemen’s Houthis fired missiles at the presidential palace complex in the southern city of Aden on Thursday, killing five people, the government said, as the Saudi-led coalition listed dozens of Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure in ⁠recent weeks.
Yemen’s prime minister, Shaya al-Zindani, ⁠and cabinet members were safe following the attack, Yemeni information minister Moammar al-Eryani said.
Witnesses told Reuters they heard loud booms near the palace.
Yemen’s cabinet said the attack involved missiles and drones.
Yemen’s health minister, Qasim Buhaibeh, said five people were killed and 16 wounded in the attack, with casualties including guards and civilian employees.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said its fighters had bombed what he described as ​the Saudi military operations headquarters in Aden, as part of the group’s declared policy ‌of targeting “Saudi reinforcements wherever they were located”.
Agence France-Presse reported that a Yemeni government minister said on condition of anonymity that the palace attack had hit a command centre for the Saudi-led coalition.

The official added that the command centre was hit by three missiles, and the headquarters of the coalition forces at the presidential complex with two missiles, adding that there were Yemeni and Saudi casualties, without providing a specific toll.

Fighting has escalated between the Houthi rebels and a Saudi-led coalition as part of clashes linked to the US and Israeli war on Iran, and aid agencies have warned of rapidly worsening conditions in Yemen.
The clashes have complicated efforts to end the wider Iran war and further rattled global markets as Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s top oil exporters, faces repeated attacks.

“The NASA-JAXA sample curation partnership is extremely valuable, and I am proud that NASA Science is supporting MMX sample curation and will be sharing portions of these samples for study as we continue to expand humanity’s understanding of the universe for the benefit of all.”
Scientists have long debated the origin of Mars’ two moons.
The data and samples collected by the MMX mission will help answer essential questions about the origins of these moons and the history of the solar system.

“Phobos and Deimos may be the remains of a massive impact on Mars that sent material into orbit around the planet, or they could be ancient asteroids that were captured by Mars’ gravity billions of years ago,” said Tom Statler, MMX program executive and program scientist at NASA Headquarters. “Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds.”
Another key part of NASA’s contribution to MMX is its scientific partnership with JAXA.

NASA-supported researchers are working alongside international colleagues to help reveal the story of Phobos and will use mission data and returned samples to uncover new clues about the moon’s origin and the evolution of the Mars system.

items.title: Pentagon seeks expertise to develop brain injury assessment standards
items.originalTitle: Pentagon seeks expertise to develop brain injury assessment standards
items.summary: The Pentagon is looking to create standards to assess the impact of blast-induced mild traumatic brain injuries. The goal is to have benchmarks that will allow assessment of the “physiological and biomechanical effects of blast injuries” caused by explosions of enemy munitions or the blast effects from firing friendly weapons, according to the Request for Information by the Blast Injury Research Coordinating Office, or BIRCO , within U.S. Army Medical Research and Development Command .

evidenceRecords.text: The Pentagon is looking to create standards to assess the impact of blast-induced mild traumatic brain injuries.

The goal is to have benchmarks that will allow assessment of the “physiological and biomechanical effects of blast injuries” caused by explosions of enemy munitions or the blast effects from firing friendly weapons, according to the Request for Information by the Blast Injury Research Coordinating Office, or BIRCO , within U.S. Army Medical Research and Development Command .

This will enable “risk assessment of military service members who are exposed to blunt impacts resulting from acceleration of the body, blunt injury from a ballistic strike to the helmet, or effects from blast pressure produced by a weapon system or explosion,” the RFI reads.
BIRCO is seeking a variety of information that can help formulate standards for assessing mild traumatic brain injuries, or mTBI.
The information could include existing criteria, standards and models for brain injuries, as well as identifying experts on the topic.

The Pentagon is also seeking input from manufacturers of protective gear that can be “highly relevant to understanding human tolerance limits and predicting blast injuries.” The RFI uses a broad definition of blast injuries, including the effects on the body of blast-wave overpressure, fragments, the human body being thrown against hard objects, collapsing buildings and burns, as well as the effects of toxic gases and radiation.

“The standards can range from simple dose response curves and injury thresholds that address single components of blast insults, such as blast pressure wave magnitude, or address multiple components of blast insults, such as pressure magnitude over time,” the RFI said.

These standards will be used for “health hazard assessments, survivability assessments, and protection system development aimed at producing safe weapon systems, survivable combat platforms, and effective protection systems.” The effects of traumatic brain injuries on military personnel have become better known in recent years.

items.title: Brazil is rewriting the rules for its drone future
items.originalTitle: Brazil is rewriting the rules for its drone future
items.summary: Brazil has spent years building a regulatory framework for drones. In June 2026, it took another significant step, replacing its previous rules with a new risk-based system designed to accommodate a wider range of civil uncrewed aircraft system (UAS) operations.1 But regulation is only one part of integrating drones into the airspace; enforcing those regulations is the other. What happens when operators do not follow the rules? Do authorities have the tools and coordination needed to respond? Brazil is now dealing with both sides of that equation.

Brazil has spent years building a regulatory framework for drones.
In June 2026, it took another significant step, replacing its previous rules with a new risk-based system designed to accommodate a wider range of civil uncrewed aircraft system (UAS) operations.1
But regulation is only one part of integrating drones into the airspace; enforcing those regulations is the other.
What happens when operators do not follow the rules?
Do authorities have the tools and coordination needed to respond?
Brazil is now dealing with both sides of that equation.
In June 2026, Brazil’s national civil aviation agency, Agência Nacional de Aviação Civil (ANAC), approved RBAC 100, replacing the previous RBAC-E 94 framework.
The new regulation moved away from a system primarily based on drone weight and introduced three categories based on the risk of the operation: open, specific and certified.1

The open category covers lower risk operations, including flights of aircraft weighing up to 25 kg, within visual or extended visual line of sight and up to 120 metres above ground level, subject to defined conditions.

Operations that do not meet the requirements of the open category fall into the specific category and require either compliance with a standard scenario established by ANAC or an operational authorisation based on a risk assessment.

ANAC’s regulatory analysis identified the consolidation of the UAS market and the need for requirements covering areas including airworthiness, operations, maintenance, training, pilot qualifications and registration.
It also proposed a performance-based approach intended to provide greater flexibility as technology and applications develop.2

The airport was selected in part because of its history of drone incidents, highlighting the need to move beyond defining the rules towards developing the capabilities needed when those rules are not followed.4

items.title: Terra Quantum Joins QuEra Quantum Alliance
items.originalTitle: Terra Quantum Joins QuEra Quantum Alliance
items.summary: Insider Brief Terra Quantum has joined the QuEra Quantum Alliance, adding its quantum software, algorithms and enterprise application expertise to the neutral-atom quantum computing partner network. Terra Quantum ‘s TQ42 platform provides a cloud-based quantum software environment with a Python SDK, APIs and algorithms for optimization, quantum machine learning and simulation. The partnership aims to connect enterprise applications with QuEra’s neutral-atom hardware, as QuEra targets availability of its 256-logical-qubit Libra fault-tolerant quantum computer through Amazon Braket in 2028.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Terra Quantum has joined the QuEra Quantum Alliance, adding its quantum software, algorithms and enterprise application expertise to the neutral-atom quantum computing partner network.
Terra Quantum ‘s TQ42 platform provides a cloud-based quantum software environment with a Python SDK, APIs and algorithms for optimization, quantum machine learning and simulation.

The partnership aims to connect enterprise applications with QuEra’s neutral-atom hardware, as QuEra targets availability of its 256-logical-qubit Libra fault-tolerant quantum computer through Amazon Braket in 2028.

PRESS RELEASE — Terra Quantum , a global leader in the development of quantum technologies and their industrial application, the leader in neutral-atom quantum computing, today announced that Terra Quantum has joined the QuEra Quantum Alliance, a global partner program dedicated to accelerating the development, deployment, and utilization of neutral-atom quantum computers to solve the world’s most challenging computational problems.
Reinforcing the Applications Layer of the QuEra Quantum Alliance Terra Quantum is hardware-agnostic by design, developing proprietary algorithms and software rather than quantum processors.

As a member of the QuEra Quantum Alliance, Terra Quantum will gain access to technical expertise and go-to-market resources from QuEra as well as partnership opportunities with other, complementary alliance members.
Both QuEra and Terra Quantum see their expanded partnership as an opportunity to shorten the distance between an enterprise use case and hardware designed to scale toward fault tolerance.
“Quantum computing will create its real economic impact when world-class hardware and world-class applications come together,” said Markus Pflitsch, Founder, Chairman and CEO of Terra Quantum .

By joining the QuEra Quantum Alliance, we are bringing our algorithms and application expertise closer to one of the most promising hardware platforms in the industry, helping turn advances in quantum computing into solutions for real-world problems.” A Growing Global Alliance The QuEra Quantum Alliance brings together quantum hardware, software, and service providers to foster collaboration and widespread adoption of neutral-atom quantum computing.
Terra Quantum joins in a year when QuEra has put a dated path to fault tolerance on the record.

Libra , QuEra’s first fault-tolerant quantum computer, is a 256 logical qubit, megaquop-class system targeted for availability on Amazon Braket in 2028, and QuEra has since detailed a next-generation gigaquop-class FTQC system.

“ Terra Quantum strengthens the software and applications layer of the QuEra Quantum Alliance, which is where most enterprise conversations actually begin,” said Yuval Boger, Chief Commercial Officer at QuEra Computing.

items.summary: Airbus recently put the demonstrator for its MQ-72C drone helicopter through the paces for the U.S. Army. The MQ-72C has been in development for several years now for a U.S. Marine Corps competition seeking a new uncrewed cargo-carrying Aerial Logistics Connector (ALC). The Marines see uncrewed logistics ‘connectors’ as key to future expeditionary and distributed operations , and a similar Army requirement could be on the horizon, especially to support long-range air assaults .

evidenceRecords.text: Airbus recently put the demonstrator for its MQ-72C drone helicopter through the paces for the U.S. Army.
The MQ-72C has been in development for several years now for a U.S. Marine Corps competition seeking a new uncrewed cargo-carrying Aerial Logistics Connector (ALC).

The Marines see uncrewed logistics ‘connectors’ as key to future expeditionary and distributed operations , and a similar Army requirement could be on the horizon, especially to support long-range air assaults .

Jaysen Yochim, Senior Director for the ALC program at Airbus, talked about the demonstration for the Army with our Howard Altman at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention on Monday.
Airbus is currently teamed with L3Harris Technologies, Shield AI, and Parry Labs on development of this drone helicopter for the Marines, as you can learn more about here .
The current iteration of the MQ-72C is based on the crewed UH-72B Lakota, which is in turn a variant of Airbus’ H145 twin-engine light helicopter.
The Army operates crewed UH-72s today , but only in non-combat roles, including counter-drug and border patrol missions, and almost exclusively within the borders of the United States.
US Army crewed UH-72 Lakota helicopters.
US Army The MQ-72C demonstration for the Army, which Airbus self-funded, took place last week at Huntsville Executive Airport just outside of Huntsville, Alabama.

“We did multiple traffic patterns to demonstrate just a normal traffic pattern, like a normal day would be, but also traffic patterns or a flight with a no-fly zone popping up in the middle of the flight.” The video below shows previous flight testing of the MQ-72C demonstrator.
In that latter instance, the MQ-72C had to “autonomously make decisions” about how it was “going to route itself around the no-fly zones” once they popped up, he added.
Though the demonstrator now has provisions for a pilot, the intention is for the MQ-72C to eventually operate in a completely uncrewed mode.

evidenceRecords.text: Shield AI delivers the first V-BAT autonomous aircraft to the Taiwan Coast Guard Administration, enhancing maritime domain awareness with partner AIDC.

Shield AI press release Defense-tech company Shield AI announced the first delivery of its V-BAT to the Taiwan Coast Guard Administration (CGA) with its partner Aerospace Industrial Development Corporation (AIDC).
Shield AI’s V-BATs were competitively selected by the CGA in July 2026 for its “Shipborne UAV” program.
Shield AI engineers demonstrated aircraft setup within minutes, displaying V-BAT’s ease of operations and advanced technological capabilities for maritime security.
CGA will utilize V-BAT as a ship-based capability to maintain persistent Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) for surveillance, coastal patrols and law enforcement operations.
Vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) aircraft eliminate the need for runways and improve deployment flexibility while optimizing costs and reducing personnel requirements.
Partnering to build local expertise, Shield AI will train Coast Guard operators and maintenance personnel while simultaneously creating a robust localized support system for the V-BATs with AIDC.

“V-BAT will give Taiwan’s Coast Guard the maritime domain awareness and intelligence picture needed across the Taiwan Strait and its maritime borders,” said Brandon Tseng, Shield AI president and co-founder.
“V-BAT already does this for the U.S. Coast Guard, helping intercept more than 100,000 pounds of narcotics last year alone.
Extending those same capabilities to Taiwan helps keep the Strait safe from illegal activity and hostile actors.

It gives Taiwan the sovereignty it needs to protect its own waters.” Last year, Shield AI and AIDC entered into an agreement to advance Taiwan’s sovereign defense capabilities, strengthen its aerospace industrial base, and enhance collaborative technological innovation.

The companies have engaged in strategic collaboration through sustainment, training, autonomy integration, and other technical initiatives to ensure Shield AI’s products can be deployed, supported, and scaled in Taiwan.

The comments marked Trump’s first definitive statement on the nuclear topic following speculation about a possible atomic conflict earlier in the US and Israel’s war on Iran.
They also appeared to confirm speculation that another phase of the war is imminent, likely after the US midterm elections on November 3.

Trump told Newsmax that the US might indeed launch another strike on Iran’s nuclear sites, particularly on Pickaxe Mountain, where Tehran is believed to be hiding a nuclear facility deep under layers of granite.
“Well, the mother of all bombs is not nuclear,” Trump said. “It’s not nuclear at all.
This is just an extremely large bomb.”
Trump also suggested renewed attacks are likely in the near future.
The US cannot end the war now because it has to ensure Iran cannot produce a nuclear weapon, he argued, saying he believes that “if they had it, they would use it, in my opinion, instantaneously”.
However, Magnier said there is doubt about whether using the massive surface explosive would be effective against deeply buried nuclear installations in Iran.
“Well, the mother of all bombs is not nuclear,” Trump said.
Trump has never explicitly mentioned using a nuclear weapon, but he has also never ruled it out.

With Trump failing to rule out dropping the MOAB, analysts speculate that the US might launch another – perhaps final – intensive bombing campaign targeting Iran’s nuclear and defence sites, particularly Pickaxe Mountain.

items.title: ENAIRE and partners discuss next steps for U-space in Benidorm
items.originalTitle: ENAIRE and partners discuss next steps for U-space in Benidorm
items.summary: Spanish air navigation services provider ENAIRE, the Benidorm City Council and the Polytechnic University of Valencia met on 15 October to discuss U-space in Benidorm. ENAIRE also provided an uncrewed traffic management demonstration. The meeting was held with the intention of bringing administrations, operators, users and agents of the sector closer to the safe and efficient integration of drones in the airspace.

evidenceRecords.text: Spanish air navigation services provider ENAIRE, the Benidorm City Council and the Polytechnic University of Valencia met on 15 October to discuss U-space in Benidorm.
For more information ENAIRE The post ENAIRE and partners discuss next steps for U-space in Benidorm first appeared on Unmanned airspace .
ENAIRE also provided an uncrewed traffic management demonstration.
The meeting was held with the intention of bringing administrations, operators, users and agents of the sector closer to the safe and efficient integration of drones in the airspace.

Institutional representatives and national and international experts analysed the current state of U-space services, the European regulatory framework and the new opportunities opened up by the operation of uncrewed aircraft in urban environments.

During the morning, EUROCONTROL specialists presented the evolution of the U-space project in Europe, while representatives of the Directorate General of Civil Aviation presented the progress of the National Action Plan for the Deployment of U-space and zoning (2026-2030 (PANDU+), an initiative aimed at facilitating the coordinated deployment of these services.
ENAIRE and the Polytechnic University of Valencia discussed the implications of U-space for drone operators and manned aviation.

The session addressed key aspects such as new operating procedures, safety benefits, requirements for UAS operations, available aeronautical information and the role of the Geozone Manager in airspace management.
ENAIRE presented a practical simulation of the U-space services through a demonstration of the digital platform that enables the safe and coordinated management of drone operations.
Attendees were able to experience processes such as flight plan activation, automated alert management and interaction with dynamic geographic areas.
Benidorm has a growing role as a laboratory for the development of advanced air mobility in Europe.

In February 2025, Benidorm hosted the first simultaneous operation in Europe involving an uncrewed air taxi and multiple drones in an urban environment managed through U-space services under the European U-ELCOME project.

ENAIRE said that yesterday’s event detailed how the progress demonstrated in that project is being progressively transferred from the experimental to the operational level, bringing administrations, operators and citizens closer to the capabilities that will make the safe expansion of drone operations possible in the cities of the future.

The Advantage2 system features more than 4,400 qubits and is intended to support applications in optimization, materials simulation and other industrial workloads. PRESS RELEASE — D-Wave Quantum Inc. (NASDAQ: QBTS) (“ D-Wave ” or the “Company”), the only dual-platform quantum computing company providing annealing and gate-model systems, software and services, today announced at Digital Innovation Forum 2026 that its Advantage2 TM annealing quantum computer has arrived in Lombardy, Italy, for installation at Villa Saporiti in Como.
The VoltaB1 Advantage2 annealing quantum computer will be formally inaugurated at Q-Alliance’s “ Quantum per l’Italia ” event on October 16, at the historic Villa Saporiti.
“Bringing Italy’s first annealing quantum computer to Como marks a historic milestone toward making quantum computing a working capability for Italian innovation and industry,” said Dr. Baratz.
That is how quantum infrastructure becomes industrial advantage.” The system’s arrival follows a €10 million agreement between D-Wave and SQT to deploy an annealing quantum computer in Europe.
Once operational, the Advantage2 system will be accessible through D – Wave’s Leap real-time quantum cloud service, which offers 99.9% availability and uptime.
“The arrival of the Advantage2 system in Lombardy puts physical infrastructure behind our vision for Italian quantum innovation,” said Thomas F.

“Our investment is intended to connect researchers and businesses with advanced computing resources, support the development of useful applications and help build the expertise that will sustain Italy’s role in the quantum economy.” Featuring more than 4,400 qubits, the Advantage2 system is D-Wave ’s most advanced annealing quantum computer and has demonstrated the ability to outperform classical computing on a complex materials simulation problem that would have taken one of the world’s most powerful classical supercomputers nearly one million years and the world’s annual electricity

Today, some of the world’s largest organizations across aviation, manufacturing, telecommunications and health care are using the Advantage2 system to address real-world problems, spanning optimization, materials simulation and artificial intelligence.

ADI is developing its Emerging Tech Hub within the Analog Garage to help robotics startups and established companies overcome these challenges.
The Emerging Tech Hub is intended to give companies access to ADI engineers, prototyping and testing resources, and manufacturing and sourcing expertise as they prepare their designs for production.

The challenges of scaling robotics innovation ADI was recently highlighted in The Race to Make AI Physical whitepaper explaining how physical AI brings together sensing, signal conversion, perception, reasoning, control, computing, and validation.
ADI describes this through four stages: Idea, Prototype, Validate, and Scale.
These changing demands for a robotics startup are the gaps ADI’s Emerging Tech Hub is intended to address.

The Emerging Tech Hub brings expertise and resources The Emerging Tech Hub is a robotics-focused initiative being developed to bring startups and established robotics companies closer to ADI’s technical teams, including engineers implementing newly released or still-in-development technologies.
The engineering support from ADI will depend on the robotics company’s stage and needs.

For example, a mature robotics developer might need a particular semiconductor component, while another may be trying to solve a different engineering problem, prompting the Emerging Tech Hub to find specialists within ADI.
Villone said ADI has recruited robotics experts from across the industry to be better equipped to handle fast paced robotic development.

items.title: Google Demonstrates Method to Cut Errors in Quantum Computing’s ‘Magic States’
items.originalTitle: Google Demonstrates Method to Cut Errors in Quantum Computing’s ‘Magic States’
items.summary: Insider Brief Google demonstrated magic-state cultivation on its Willow quantum processor, reducing state-preparation errors about 40-fold and reporting 99.99% logical fidelity, potentially lowering resource demands for error-corrected computing. The team used reinforcement learning to improve processor calibration and developed a measurement technique to avoid overstating the prepared states’ quality.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Google demonstrated magic-state cultivation on its Willow quantum processor, reducing state-preparation errors about 40-fold and reporting 99.99% logical fidelity, potentially lowering resource demands for error-corrected computing.
The team used reinforcement learning to improve processor calibration and developed a measurement technique to avoid overstating the prepared states’ quality.

Researchers transferred prepared states between two error-correcting codes, but larger demonstrations remain necessary, and a storage test produced errors about seven times higher than simulations predicted.
Google researchers reduced errors in a crucial quantum computing resource about 40-fold, demonstrating a method that could lower the hardware demands of useful, error-corrected machines.

The experiment, published in Science , showed that a technique called magic-state cultivation works on Google ’s Willow processor , according to a Google Quantum AI blog post written by Emma Rosenfeld, research scientist and Craig Gidney, quantum software engineer.
The team reported producing states known as T-states with a logical fidelity of 99.99%, which is a measure of how closely a protected quantum state matches its intended form.
The result addresses a problem in quantum computing that preparing these states could consume much of a future machine’s resources and leave less capacity for the calculations it is meant to perform.
Google ’s demonstration moves a proposed way to reduce that burden from theory to hardware.

The researchers were also able to transfer these prepared states between two forms of quantum error correction as an early test of whether the preparation method can connect with the architecture intended to support larger computations.
The work does not necessarily establish that the resource problem has been solved at a practical scale.

Ultimately, then, this looks to be an important, incremental advance toward practical quantum computing that demonstrates a way to prepare essential quantum states with fewer errors and potentially lower hardware demands.
According to Google ’s post, some estimates suggest that making magic states could occupy as much as 95% of a quantum computer’s capacity.

items.originalTitle: Fortem’s DroneHunter nets a bigger role in allied air defense
items.summary: Fortem Technologies and MBDA are expanding their partnership to bring autonomous counter-drone systems into air defense networks used by military and government customers across Europe and allied markets worldwide. The expanded agreement builds on a technical collaboration launched in 2024, when the companies integrated Fortem’s DroneHunter autonomous interceptor into MBDA’s Sky Warden counter-uncrewed aircraft systems (C-UAS) architecture.

evidenceRecords.text: Fortem Technologies and MBDA are expanding their partnership to bring autonomous counter-drone systems into air defense networks used by military and government customers across Europe and allied markets worldwide.

The expanded agreement builds on a technical collaboration launched in 2024, when the companies integrated Fortem’s DroneHunter autonomous interceptor into MBDA’s Sky Warden counter-uncrewed aircraft systems (C-UAS) architecture. more…

The expanded agreement builds on a technical collaboration launched in 2024, when the companies integrated Fortem’s DroneHunter autonomous interceptor into MBDA’s Sky Warden counter-uncrewed aircraft systems (C-UAS) architecture.
Now, MBDA will offer DroneHunter to its customers, allowing them to add the interceptor to their existing air defense networks instead of deploying an entirely separate system.
Sales will remain subject to applicable export authorizations.

The companies are also jointly offering FireThorn, an autonomous interceptor they developed together to counter one-way attack drones and other hostile uncrewed aircraft, including Shahed/Geran and Orlan platforms.
The two systems offer different approaches to dealing with aerial threats.
DroneHunter uses a net to capture hostile drones, making it an option for environments where minimizing collateral damage matters or where operators want to recover a drone intact for evidence.
FireThorn, meanwhile, is designed for more demanding engagements, using Fortem’s high-speed, radar-guided autonomous airframe and an MBDA NATO-approved warhead to destroy its target.
“Militaries don’t need another standalone gadget.
They need autonomous interceptors that plug into the architecture they already trust,” Fortem Technologies CEO Jon Gruen said in announcing the expanded partnership.
Gruen added that working with MBDA gives allied forces a faster route to protecting troops, military bases and critical infrastructure.
The partnership reflects a broader challenge facing modern air defenses: dealing with the growing use of relatively inexpensive drones for reconnaissance and attacks.

The centre’s nine initial research projects will cover quantum networking, sensing, hardware development and applications in fields including chemistry, materials science, finance, engineering and medicine.

IonQ plans to deploy a 256-qubit Superion quantum computer and an on-campus quantum network, while Innovate UK will provide the National Quantum Computing Centre with access and computing time over three years.

PRESS RELEASE — IonQ (NYSE: IONQ), the world’s leading full-stack quantum platform and foundry, and the University of Cambridge have announced the opening of the first-ever university-based IonQ Quantum Innovation Centre.
The Centre is located at the Ray Dolby Centre, the new home of the University’s Cavendish Laboratory.
The IonQ Quantum Innovation Centre demonstrates the company’s commitment to quantum innovation and academic research within the United Kingdom.
Research at the Centre includes co-development of new quantum network nodes and sensing capabilities with the university, and a strengthening of the existing Cambridge-to-Bristol quantum network.
IonQ and the University of Cambridge first announced the partnership on March 11, 2026, supporting advanced research and workforce development for quantum technologies.

“The opening of the IonQ Quantum Innovation Centre turns a landmark agreement into a working home for quantum research inside one of the world’s most storied physics laboratories,” said Niccolo de Masi, Chairman and CEO of IonQ.

This is a long-term commitment to the United Kingdom, built for researchers, start-ups, and industry alike.” The Centre’s nine inaugural research projects will bring together Cambridge researchers and IonQ specialists to advance quantum hardware and explore new applications across science and industry.

Selected by a Joint Steering Committee comprising business and scientific leaders from both organizations, the projects combine Cambridge’s research expertise with IonQ’s capabilities in trapped-ion quantum computing, quantum networking, and device engineering.

“The official launch of the IonQ Quantum Innovation Centre is an exciting milestone in our partnership with IonQ, which will help Cambridge and the UK stay at the forefront of the quantum revolution,” said Professor Mete Atatüre, Head of the Cavendish Laboratory.

PRESS RELEASE — SEALSQ Corp (NASDAQ: LAES) (“SEALSQ” or “Company”), a company that focuses on developing and selling Semiconductors, PKI, and Post-Quantum technology hardware and software products, today announced its preliminary unaudited financial metrics for the nine-month period ended September 30, 2026 (“9M 2026”), provided an update on operational milestones, and reaffirmed its full-year 2026 revenue guidance.
9M 2026 Key Financial Metrics Revenue growth of 65%: Preliminary unaudited 9M 2026 revenue of $16.3 million, compared to $9.9 million in 9M 2025.

Revenue Drivers The 9M 2026 increase was driven primarily by: Continued strong demand for SEALSQ ‘s Vault-IC secure-element family across industrial, smart-energy IoT and P25 Radio protocol application deployments.
Nine months of consolidated revenue from IC’Alps SAS, which contributed approximately $3.8 million in 9M 2026 through custom ASIC design and secure semiconductor engineering services.
FY 2026 Revenue Outlook SEALSQ ‘s outlook statements are based on current expectations.

SEALSQ reaffirms its FY 2026 revenue growth guidance of approximately 50% to 100%, representing a range of approximately $27 million to $36 million, compared with audited FY 2025 revenue of $18 million.
Seasonal strength in Vault-IC secure-element shipments and continued growth in recurring PKI and certificate-management revenue.

Carlos Moreira, Founder, Chairman and CEO of SEALSQ , said: “Our preliminary nine-month revenue of $16.3 million represents 65% growth year-over-year, with revenue increasing sequentially in each quarter of 2026.

With approximately $465 million in liquidity, we are well positioned to fund these priorities as we prepare for post-quantum semiconductors to become a more significant contributor to revenue in 2027.” John O’Hara, CFO of SEALSQ , added: “Based on our preliminary nine-month revenue, our reaffirmed full-year 2026 revenue guidance implies fourth-quarter revenue of $11 million to $20 million.

We remain focused on converting our pipeline into production revenue and deploying capital carefully to support growth.” Post-Quantum Commercialization and Certification Progress QS7001: Following fault-injection and side-channel testing (March 2026) and NIST SP 800-90B Entropy Source Validation, Certificate #E333 (May 2026), SEALSQ targets the QS7001 V1 Common Criteria Hardware Evaluation Test Report in October 2026 and the V2 full post-quantum report in January 2027, with formal CC EAL5+ certification progressing in 2027.

ANKARA — Turkish Aerospace has completed construction of a second production line for its Anka 3 unmanned combat aerial vehicle (UCAV) that is scheduled to open in November, a company official told Breaking Defense.

The new production line will manufacture a new variant of the Anka 3 drone that features a larger airframe and an expected payload capacity of 1.75 tons, up from about 1.3 tons on the original platform.
According to the Turkish Aerospace official, the upgraded aircraft will be able to carry more munitions to meet new national requirements.
During a visit to the company’s Ankara facility on Wednesday, the official said the second production line will allow Turkish Aerospace to produce one Anka 3 every five months.
The first aircraft to be built on the new line is expected to roll out “soon” and undergo flight testing afterward, they added.
The Anka 3 is a combat drone designed for strike and other missions.
The aircraft can reach high-subsonic speeds and operate at altitudes of up to 40,000 feet, according to Turkish Aerospace.
The Turkish armed forces ordered 80 Anka 3 UCAVs, with first delivery expected in 2027.
Media were invited to cover Atış Serbest exercise in Turkey and tour facilities of five defense firms: Aselsan, Turkish Aerospace, Asfat, MKE and Roketsan.
Breaking Defense accepted travel and accommodation from Turkish Ministry of Defense.
During the media tour, reporters had a closer look at the first prototype of the original Anka 3 drone, which is currently in flight testing.
Just next to the Anka 3 prototype were Turkish Aerospace’s newly unveiled Ayaz turbojet-powered one-way attack UAV and the company’s Super Şimşek kamikaze drone.

items.title: What is the US Army doing in Panama? A bit of everything.
items.originalTitle: What is the US Army doing in Panama? A bit of everything.
items.summary: Typically a country may host a U.S. Army Civil Affairs team or two — the Army’s special operations forces contingent that connects military forces with civilian populations — but Panama is home to an entire U.S. Civil Affairs company, White said, that works in virtually every district. Those teams, he said, identify gaps in civilian infrastructure, such as dilapidated schools or unsafe bridges. The U.S. has military salvage dive teams operating around the canal and cross-training with Panamanian forces. Engineer soldiers rotate through the country, building out structures for jungle students.

evidenceRecords.text: Typically a country may host a U.S. Army Civil Affairs team or two — the Army’s special operations forces contingent that connects military forces with civilian populations — but Panama is home to an entire U.S. Civil Affairs company, White said, that works in virtually every district.
The U.S. has military salvage dive teams operating around the canal and cross-training with Panamanian forces.
Military doctors work alongside Panamanian medical professionals to assist local populations, performing colonoscopies and cataract surgeries.
White said one of the lessons the U.S. learned during its decades-long wars in Iraq and Afghanistan was that the military cannot quickly create trust.

“And so, being here — present — doing things on the regular with SENAFRONT and SENAN, with the government of Panama — and with their permission to do it — it helps build that trust.” Though Panama does not have a standing Army, SENAFRONT and SENAN are two branches of the Panamanian Public Forces.
Those teams, he said, identify gaps in civilian infrastructure, such as dilapidated schools or unsafe bridges.
Engineer soldiers rotate through the country, building out structures for jungle students.
Dentists and optometrists — even veterinarians — rotate through rural parts of the country.

“In a crisis, you simply can’t surge trust,” he said. “And so, being here — present — doing things on the regular with SENAFRONT and SENAN, with the government of Panama — and with their permission to do it — it helps build that trust.” Though Panama does not have a standing Army, SENAFRONT and SENAN are two branches of the Panamanian Public Forces.
With terrain different from the U.S.’s Hawaii jungle course, Panama’s environment replicates other jungle biomes where the U.S. may find itself in conflict.
The Western Hemisphere, White said, abounds with jungle landscape.
Officials have been adamant that the future does not hold permanent military basing for U.S. troops.
White said the U.S. contingent works to uphold the Neutrality Treaty of 1977 — which guarantees the Panama Canal remains neutral and open for ships of all nations to transit peacefully.

PRESS RELEASE — A quantum technology invented at the State University of New York (SUNY) at Stony Brook (Stony Brook University) is earning international recognition.

Qunnect ’s Qu-MEM, a commercial room-temperature quantum memory device developed from Stony Brook-patented technology, has been named to TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026 in the Experimental category for concept inventions and prototypes showing future potential.
This recognition highlights Stony Brook’s role in advancing quantum technology and demonstrates how university research can move beyond the laboratory to help shape emerging industries.

Qunnect ’s Qu-MEM grew out of research led by Professor Eden Figueroa, Stony Brook’s Endowed Presidential Professor of Physics and director of the Stony Brook University Quantum Institute alongside alumni/graduate students Mehdi Namazi, PhD ’18, and Mael Flament, MS ’19.
Qu-MEM is the world’s first commercial room-temperature quantum memory device, currently expanding Stony Brook’s SCY-QNET, America’s largest quantum internet.

King Jr. said, “The State University of New York at Stony Brook has emerged as a global leader in quantum technology and research through the strong investment by Governor Hochul, state leaders, and SUNY, and thanks to world-class researchers, faculty, and students who are moving this field forward.

I applaud the State University of New York at Stony Brook on this well-earned recognition, which reinforces that investments made in SUNY research help move our state and society forward.” “ Stony Brook University is proud to celebrate Qunnect ’s recognition by TIME for creating one of the year’s best inventions.

This quantum memory is an essential component in Stony Brook’s fiber and wireless quantum network, which is the largest metropolitan area quantum network in the world communicating quantum information via entangled photons.

This quantum network, which we plan to grow first to upstate New York and then throughout the country, is capable of protecting sensitive data in critical sectors including healthcare, finance and national defense,” said Stony Brook University President Andrea Goldsmith.

PRESS RELEASE — CEOs, CTOs, and founders from nine blockchain organizations today launched the Quantum Alliance , an open standards body that will set the criteria for judging quantum-resistance claims in blockchain and create standards for compatibility between the networks as they migrate.
The Alliance will define what post-quantum readiness means for blockchain networks, wallets, and infrastructure, and how to test and verify any claim of quantum resistance.

Nearly every major blockchain secures its accounts with elliptic-curve signatures, and once an account signs a transaction (for some address types, from the moment it is created), its public key sits permanently on a public ledger.
A sufficiently capable quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm could work backward from that public key to the private key and take control of the funds.
The same signatures protect stablecoin minting keys, governance contracts, bridges, and oracle feeds, so one compromised privileged key could spread across many platforms at once.
The Quantum Alliance was formed to set that bar.

items.title: Rigorous Analysis Confirms NASA’s Artemis II Heat Shield Performance
items.originalTitle: Rigorous Analysis Confirms NASA’s Artemis II Heat Shield Performance
items.summary: Additional engineering data analysis of the Orion spacecraft’s heat shield confirmed initial data showing the heat shield performed as expected. After NASA’s thorough analysis of Artemis I heat shield findings , informed by extensive arc jet material testing at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley, the agency modified Orion’s reentry trajectory for Artemis II by shortening the maximum downrange distance the spacecraft could fly between when it entered Earth’s atmosphere and splashed down in the Pacific Ocean.

evidenceRecords.text: Additional engineering data analysis of the Orion spacecraft’s heat shield confirmed initial data showing the heat shield performed as expected.

After NASA’s thorough analysis of Artemis I heat shield findings , informed by extensive arc jet material testing at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley, the agency modified Orion’s reentry trajectory for Artemis II by shortening the maximum downrange distance the spacecraft could fly between when it entered Earth’s atmosphere and splashed down in the Pacific Ocean.

Analysis prior to the mission showed that limiting downrange distance would limit how long the spacecraft’s heat shield spent in the temperature range at which the Artemis I heat shield phenomenon occurred.
Shortly after Artemis II splashdown on April 10, 2026, U.S. Navy divers captured underwater imagery of the Orion spacecraft’s heat shield.

Initial inspections of the thermal protection system, including diver imagery of the spacecraft’s heat shield taken just after splashdown and further inspections on the recovery ship, found it performed as expected, with a significant reduction in the amount of cracks and char loss as compared to Artemis I.

Upon the spacecraft’s return to NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida after the Moon mission, thermal protection system experts began additional examination of the heat shield, made of 186 unique blocks of an ablative material called Avcoat.

The heat shield was then transported to NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, where work on sample extraction and internal x-ray scans began in August to provide further engineering insight into the system and behavior of the material.

NASA/Kevin Davis A thorough post-flight assessment review found that Orion’s aerodynamic and aerothermal performance, including the heat shield and backshell thermal protection system, was in line with engineering predictions based on pre-flight analyses and ground testing.

The shorter allowable down range during entry reduced the cracking and char loss experienced on the Artemis II heat shield relative to the Artemis I heat shield by a factor of ten, proving the effectiveness of the trajectory modification.
Engineers found only nine spots of char loss of varying sizes on the Artemis II heat shield dish, compared to 103 during Artemis I.

The analysis also showed that Orion’s robust heat shield design showed consistency from Artemis I to Artemis II, evident by the performance of system features such as the seams between the heat shield Avcoat blocks and the Avcoat surrounding the heat shield compression pad separation bolts.

The team also performed post-flight laser scans of the heat shield surface and is comparing this data to pre-flight measurements to determine material recession, which will then be compared to analysis predictions.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Army’s top commander for the Western Hemisphere described American “economic supremacy” as an overarching goal of Washington’s regional security strategy, outlining plans to expand its military footprint in Central and South America on Monday at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting .
The 2025 National Security Strategy prioritizes economic dominance in the Western Hemisphere through national security, Gen.
Joseph Ryan, the commander of the U.S. Army Western Hemisphere Command, said during a panel discussion with Gen.

“The end state is economic supremacy for the United States,” Ryan said, later adding, “We have ceded control of that economic terrain in this hemisphere to the People’s Republic of China over at least the last two decades, and that is a major threat to our national security.” Ryan pointed to Panama as an example, explaining how a high percentage of trade to and from the United States passes through the Panama Canal.

Ryan said the task force would receive more rotary-wing aircraft and personnel to “address some of the natural disasters and threats in the region.” Those additional resources, he said, “become absolutely critical when you’re talking about moving supplies, moving people to the point of need, and making assessments.” Command restructure In a major force restructure, the Army stood up the Western Hemisphere Command in December 2025, combining U.S. Army North, U.S. Army South and Armed Forces Command under a single headquarters.

evidenceRecords.text: HII announced that its Newport News Shipbuilding (NNS) division was awarded a $56 million contract by the U.S. Navy for shipbuilding engineering and design in support of the trilateral Australia, United Kingdom, and United States (AUKUS) partnership.
HII press release The contract includes an option which, if exercised, would bring the cumulative value of this contract to $91 million.
HII continues to take a whole-company approach to support the AUKUS agreement, providing services and support for AUKUS across its business divisions.

Under the contract, in support of Foreign Military Sales (FMS) requirements, NNS will continue supporting the United Kingdom and Australia, including technology insertion, engineering, supply chain and workforce development support, and digital transformation.

The award also includes the United States Industry Support (USIS) effort, wherein NNS engineers and designers will support the design of the SSN-AUKUS nuclear-powered submarine to be built by the United Kingdom and Australia.
“Our longstanding nuclear experience at NNS directly benefits the AUKUS mission to support shared security objectives,” said Bryan Caccavale, NNS vice president of program management.

“We are honored to leverage that experience and contribute even more to the AUKUS partnership.” The contract award is the latest in a range of initiatives HII is actively engaged in to advance the AUKUS partnership.

HII’s Mission Technologies division in Australia was awarded the contract to deliver the Australian Submarine Supplier Qualification (AUSSQ) Program , which accelerates the identification, development and qualification of Australian suppliers for integration into the United States submarine industrial base.
HII is also working with Australian industry and academia in Australia to develop the skilled workforce needed to support Australia’s nuclear-powered submarine enterprise.

The company was also awarded the Australian Submarine Agency’s Nuclear Capability Advisory Services (ANCAS) contract in December 2025 to support development of Australia’s Nuclear Power Submarine (NPS) programs through nuclear program management and technical support services. – End –

items.title: NASA Satellites Observe Historic 2026 El Niño
items.originalTitle: NASA Satellites Observe Historic 2026 El Niño
items.summary: El Niño is a natural climate pattern that emerges roughly every two to seven years marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific. NASA scientists are keeping watch as it flips trade winds, redistributes ocean heat, scrambles rain patterns, and raises sea surface height across parts of the Pacific. Follow along with these maps as NASA tracks El Niño from its epicenter in the equatorial Pacific Ocean.

evidenceRecords.text: 6 Min Read NASA Satellites Observe Historic 2026 El Niño This visualization compares three ocean data products, sea surface temperature anomaly, apparent visible wavelength, and sea surface height anomaly, over the same months in 2025 and 2026.
Credits: NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio A phenomenon rarer than a solar eclipse and more powerful than any single storm system is unfolding this fall, and NASA is tracking it closely.
El Niño is a natural climate pattern that emerges roughly every two to seven years marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific.
NASA scientists are keeping watch as it flips trade winds, redistributes ocean heat, scrambles rain patterns, and raises sea surface height across parts of the Pacific.
Follow along with these maps as NASA tracks El Niño from its epicenter in the equatorial Pacific Ocean.
“Kelvin waves are like the heartbeat of El Niño,” said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California.
Credit: NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio Warmer-than-normal seawater is one of the best-known indicators of El Niño.
Credit: NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio El Niño’s warm waters also change the color of the ocean.
One of the first clues appeared in satellite imagery in January 2026, when a swell of warm water called a Kelvin wave was spotted near Micronesia in the western Pacific.
Kelvin waves are slow-moving pulses of water thousands of miles long.
Like underwater freeways, they transfer heat from west to east across the Pacific.
The warm water heats the air directly above it, making it rise.

The change in air pressures weakens or even reverses the trade winds that typically blow in the opposing direction, from the Americas toward Asia, causing sea levels in the eastern Pacific to rise further, and waters to warm even more.
The map above shows that by early April, those Kelvin waves had reached the eastern Pacific, and sea surface temperatures had begun to warm.
Warm water expands in volume, elevating local sea levels in some areas by as much as 1 to 1.3 feet (30 to 40 centimeters).
The higher-than-normal water can be seen sloshing toward South America then moving up the coast to California.

“Kelvin waves are like the heartbeat of El Niño,” said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “And our sea level satellites let us peer into the ocean and watch every beat.”
NASA scientists will continue to monitor the signs and impacts of this El Niño with its fleet of Earth-observing satellites.

items.originalTitle: Expanded dining options popular among soldiers, US Army officials say
items.summary: The U.S. Army is continuing to roll out pilot programs aimed at improving soldiers’ diets, including expanded, campus-like dining hall options and partnerships with restaurant franchises — and reporting high soldier satisfaction with the changes. “Chow halls operated on decades-old schedules that clashed with modern soldier work shifts,” Jason Condrey, acting deputy chief of staff of Army Materiel Command, said Wednesday at the Association of the United States Army annual meeting in Washington, D.C.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Army is continuing to roll out pilot programs aimed at improving soldiers’ diets, including expanded, campus-like dining hall options and partnerships with restaurant franchises — and reporting high soldier satisfaction with the changes.

“Chow halls operated on decades-old schedules that clashed with modern soldier work shifts,” Jason Condrey, acting deputy chief of staff of Army Materiel Command, said Wednesday at the Association of the United States Army annual meeting in Washington, D.C.

Changing how, when and where service members can eat is an ongoing process, with new programs, such as flexible eating and extended dining (FEED) and campus-style dining venues (CSDV), available at select Army installations in the continental U.S. CSDVs launched in September 2025 and are currently available at five different Army installations: Fort Bragg, North Carolina; Fort Stewart, Georgia; ort.
They are operated by private contractors, unlike traditional garrison dining halls that are operated by the base and staffed by soldiers.
The panel of Army officials on Wednesday touted the popularity of the new dining facilities.

Changing how, when and where service members can eat is an ongoing process, with new programs, such as flexible eating and extended dining (FEED) and campus-style dining venues (CSDV), available at select Army installations in the continental U.S.
CSDVs launched in September 2025 and are currently available at five different Army installations: Fort Bragg, North Carolina; Fort Stewart, Georgia; ort.
Carson, Colorado; Fort Hood, Texas; and Fort Drum, New York.
“[At] Fort Carson alone ... we’re looking at about 67% utilization from the soldiers that live in the barracks, and another 56% for the soldiers that live at Fort Hood,” Sgt.
Damarco Wyatt of Army Materiel Command said.
Dependents can dine with their soldiers at CSDVs, Wyatt added, though they still must pay for their meals.
Traditional garrison dining halls typically allow dependents only under specific circumstances, like holidays.

“If we look at the two that have been open the longest — at Hood and at Carson — Hood’s a very large installation, and yet the Army is serving about 55% of its meals from the CSDV,” said Sydney Smith, director of materiel management at the Office of the Deputy Chief of Staff. “At Carson, about 85% of meals are being served out of that one CSDV.”

items.originalTitle: Museum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashed
items.summary: A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane. The black-and-white images were published by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand after renewed interest in one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century, spurred by a US expedition to the Pacific atoll of Nikumaroro in search of new clues.

evidenceRecords.text: Images from New Zealand aerial survey of Nikumaroro in 1938 offer new clues over aviator’s disappearance A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane.

The black-and-white images were published by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand after renewed interest in one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century, spurred by a US expedition to the Pacific atoll of Nikumaroro in search of new clues.

A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane.

While some low-resolution copies have been uploaded on blogs, the Air Force Museum of New Zealand said it had received several requests for the photos and had released the full set of 47 images in digital high-resolution format on its website.

Earhart’s most prominent investigator, Ric Gillespie, described the images as a “goldmine” in his blog, saying they were a complete set of aerial photos taken on 1 December 1938 by an amphibious biplane during a New Zealand survey of Pacific islands that was looking for suitable airbase locations.

A leading theory is that the aviator, who broke several records including becoming the first woman to fly a nonstop solo trip across the Atlantic, ran out of fuel and was marooned on Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.

This week, archaeologists and scientists from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University in Indianapolis, are searching a part of the island for the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape in a lagoon named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image.

items.title: Starlink: How Elon Musk's company influences geopolitics
items.originalTitle: Starlink: How Elon Musk's company influences geopolitics
items.summary: Starlink was initially developed by the American tech billionaire Elon Musk to solve this problem. It was designed as a way of quickly getting the internet into regions all over the world where this was either impossible to do by conventional methods, or so expensive that it wasn't worth attempting. Since then, Starlink's field of application has widened significantly. It's used as a means of communication in disaster zones, but also by armies or protest movements, for example in regions where the existing internet has been destroyed by enemy fire or shut down by authoritarian governments.

evidenceRecords.text: Designed to bring internet access to remote regions, Elon Musk's Starlink has become vital in crisis regions and war zones.

Since then, Starlink's field of application has widened significantly.

It's used as a means of communication in disaster zones, but also by armies or protest movements, for example in regions where the existing internet has been destroyed by enemy fire or shut down by authoritarian governments.
But there is a downside: Ukraine's military, for example, is heavily dependent on Musk's satellite system.
This has become especially apparent as the service faces external disruption.
Starlink, which is operated by Musk's SpaceX company, is a satellite-based system consisting of 10,000 small satellites located around the world.
They transfer data packages via laser links and do not require a constant, direct visual link to a ground station.
In mid-October, Ukrainian army units reported disruptions to data transmission, which are said to have severely affected the control of combat, interceptor- and reconnaissance drones.
Elon Musk said that restrictions on the speed and use of Starlink are determined by the US military and ultimately the US president.
At this stage, it remains unclear who ordered the restrictions.
Starlink is often the only way to access the internet in conflict zones.
Elon Musk also has competition inside the US from another billionaire, Jeff Bezos, whose company Amazon is currently working on Amazon Leo, known until recently as Project Kuiper.
