items.title: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
items.originalTitle: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
items.summary: US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad. Trump had previously said he approved of showing the death of the Fort Hood attacker, while Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt on whether it would happen and said he would not watch it. Trump's decision to cancel the livestream came after widespread criticism in the US and globally. On Thursday, he said that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die".

evidenceRecords.text: US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad.
Trump had previously said he approved of showing the death of the Fort Hood attacker, while Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt on whether it would happen and said he would not watch it.
Trump's decision to cancel the livestream came after widespread criticism in the US and globally.
On Thursday, he said that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die".
"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," Trump said.
"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," the president added in the post on Truth Social.
Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US military personnel and injured 32 others at a military base in Texas in 2009.
His execution by firing squad will be the first military execution in more than 60 years.
Trump said the families of the victims can still view the execution in person if they wish.

After the Pentagon announced last week that it would execute Hasan on 3 December 2026 by firing squad and livestream the event, a cascade of criticism quickly followed from human rights groups and many others.
The United Nations called the plans "abhorrent".
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth defended his decision to air Hasan's execution online, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things".

But as criticism mounted, Trump appeared to hedge his support, saying on Friday that he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but adding that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.
The president also called Hasan "totally nuts".
After Trump announced he called it off, a Pentagon spokesman said Hegseth had spoken with the US president beforehand.

items.title: Meta launches an open-weight AI model that runs on Macs
items.originalTitle: Meta launches an open-weight AI model that runs on Macs
items.summary: Meta has launched what it calls the “most capable” open-weight model in the United States. Dubbed Muse Spark Open, the model also has the distinction of having been designed to work with Macs. The new model, which leverages 816 billion parameters and a 1 million token context window, claims to offer superior performance to other popular open-weight models, according to evaluation results released by Meta on Thursday. Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and built for complex coding tasks and agentic labor. It has also been designed to run locally on Apple’s computers.

It has also been designed to run locally on Apple’s computers.
However, you will still need a lot of power to run the model locally, with a requirement of at least 1 terabyte of RAM, per Engadget.
The model will run best via the Mac Studio that comes equipped with the M5 Ultra chip.
Still, if you can muster the memory, Muse Spark Open may prove a significant work horse for coding and other desktop tasks.

Meta says that it paired the model with Muse Code, its AI coding terminal, and deployed it to various agentic workflows, including coding fixes for a Mastodon client that included “bug fixes, new features, [and] full build.”
The company says it also deployed it in the service of running DaVinci Resolve, the high-end video editing software, revealing that the model was capable of reviewing and cropping footage.
Open-weight models provide a number of distinct industry advantages that aren’t afforded by closed and proprietary models.
Open-weight models can be significantly more cost-efficient and can also offer transparency and flexibility that closed source models don’t allow.

items.title: Early tests show fiber-optic sensors could flag cracks in nuclear fuel storage canisters
items.originalTitle: Early tests show fiber-optic sensors could flag cracks in nuclear fuel storage canisters
items.summary: Researchers at the University of Pittsburgh Swanson School of Engineering have partnered with Pittsburgh startup Sensible Photonics, co-founded by Pitt professor Paul Ohodnicki, to develop a fiber-optic ultrasonic acoustic-sensing system that can detect corrosion and cracking in steel nuclear fuel storage canisters. From Sept. 8 to 11, the Pitt team of Ohodnicki, Khurram Naeem and Yang-Duan Su conducted field testing of an early concept of the technology at the Idaho National Laboratory (INL) in Idaho Falls, Idaho.

evidenceRecords.text: Researchers at the University of Pittsburgh Swanson School of Engineering have partnered with Pittsburgh startup Sensible Photonics, co-founded by Pitt professor Paul Ohodnicki, to develop a fiber-optic ultrasonic acoustic-sensing system that can detect corrosion and cracking in steel nuclear fuel storage canisters.

From Sept. 8 to 11, the Pitt team of Ohodnicki, Khurram Naeem and Yang-Duan Su conducted field testing of an early concept of the technology at the Idaho National Laboratory (INL) in Idaho Falls, Idaho.
The tests demonstrated the feasibility of the system, which has the potential to keep nuclear energy plants and surrounding communities safer.

"People tend to think about fiber optics as a way to produce faster internet speeds, but it can be used to continuously monitor everything from bridges to batteries to nuclear waste," said Naeem, technical lead on the demonstrations and a research assistant professor in mechanical engineering and materials science.
"We have developed and now demonstrated a system that can detect signals above 100 kilohertz, which can be retrofitted onto casks used to hold spent nuclear fuel.
Most conventional counterpart systems have a 20-kilohertz capability."
At nuclear reactor sites, spent fuel is cooled in water and then sealed into steel canisters, which are encased in concrete casks that can remain onsite for decades.
Even after cooling, spent fuel generates heat, so the casks include vents.
"Many nuclear energy plants are near coasts, and these vents can let in salty air that can corrode the steel, creating cracks that could compromise the canister's integrity," said Su (Ph.D.
MEMS), a postdoctoral research associate.
The fiber-optic sensing was developed to monitor the sound produced if a steel canister began corroding and cracking, alerting officials before a dangerous accident occurred.

"At the INL, we deployed the fibers outside a mock canister using different configurations to demonstrate the sensors could detect different magnitudes of acoustic vibration, validating the sensitivity of the sensor," said Su.

evidenceRecords.text: Registration is open for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, a two-day global event on Saturday, Nov. 14 and Sunday, Nov. 15, where teams work to create solutions inspired by NASA’s most ambitious exploration goals and making use of the agency’s free and open data.
The annual challenge, often called a hackathon, is an intensive, collaborative problem-solving experience where participants tackle real-world challenges created by NASA subject matter experts.

This year’s Space Apps Challenge collectively supports three major focus areas: returning humans to the Moon, preparing for missions deeper into the solar system, and expanding understanding of the universe.
Students, scientists, engineers, designers, storytellers, technologists, and space enthusiasts of all ages and experience levels can contribute their skills.

“At NASA, science is for everyone, and we’re inviting the next generation to help tackle some of humanity’s most critical challenges in space through the NASA Space Apps Challenge,” said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington.

“Everything in NASA Science is interconnected, and this year, students from around the world can use NASA’s powerful data sets to help us build the ultimate interplanetary survival guide – supporting the science that will enable astronauts to thrive on the Moon and, eventually, Mars, while also inspiring ideas that improve everyday life on Earth and in space for the benefit of all.” Supporting lunar exploration, Artemis planning NASA continues to advance plans for a sustained human presence on the Moon through the Artemis program and Moon Base.
Several of this year’s Space Apps challenges relate to analytical tools, operational considerations, and human‑system needs relevant to lunar missions.
Registration is available at the NASA Space Apps Challenge.

evidenceRecords.text: Google's Gemini 4 Argon controls robots, generates simulations from photos or sketches, and evaluates training videos.
The article Google wants Gemini 4 Argon to be the only AI model robots need appeared first on The Decoder .
Gemini 4 Argon is Google's attempt at a single AI model that controls robots, generates interactive 3D training environments, and evaluates training data.
From simple inputs like photos or sketches, the system builds simulations where robots can practice movements before real-world deployment.
The demos still require detailed human prompting and guidance.
Argon is available through Google's paid developer access programs.
With Gemini 4 Argon, Google is pitching a single model for the full robotics pipeline.
It controls robots, builds virtual practice worlds, and grades training videos.
But the example prompts reveal just how much human hand-holding the model still needs.
A Boston Dynamics Spot robot is supposed to toss soda cans into a step-on trash bin.
Before it touches the real pedal, Gemini 4 Argon builds a virtual copy of the bin, and the robot practices balancing on three legs inside that simulation.
Only then does it attempt the task on real hardware.
Before it drops the can, two extra AI agents verify that the foot and gripper are positioned correctly.
That's how Google demos the abilities of its newest model for robotics tasks.
Google also wants Argon to serve research.
Argon is available now in Google AI Studio and the development environment Antigravity, but only for Google AI Ultra subscribers.
Google had released Gemini 4 Argon globally just days earlier.

items.originalTitle: Muse Spark Open is Meta's answer to Qwen, GLM, and Kimi in the open-weight race
items.summary: After its Llama series, Meta is returning to open-weight territory with Muse Spark Open. Meta calls it the most capable US open-weight model, built for coding and agentic tasks, with 816 billion parameters (42 billion active), up to one million tokens of context, and support for text, image, video, and audio. On benchmarks like JobBench, MCP-Atlas, HLE-Diamond, and ZeroBench, Meta says it scores well ahead of Qwen 3.8, GLM 5.3, and Kimi K3 in several categories but still falls well short of Meta's paid Muse Wonder Full models.

evidenceRecords.text: Meta's Muse Spark Open is a new open-weight model with 816 billion parameters that processes text, images, video, and audio with up to one million tokens of context.
The article Muse Spark Open is Meta's answer to Qwen, GLM, and Kimi in the open-weight race appeared first on The Decoder .
After its Llama series, Meta is returning to open-weight territory with Muse Spark Open.

Meta calls it the most capable US open-weight model, built for coding and agentic tasks, with 816 billion parameters (42 billion active), up to one million tokens of context, and support for text, image, video, and audio.

On benchmarks like JobBench, MCP-Atlas, HLE-Diamond, and ZeroBench, Meta says it scores well ahead of Qwen 3.8, GLM 5.3, and Kimi K3 in several categories but still falls well short of Meta's paid Muse Wonder Full models.
The model is optimized for Apple's M5 Ultra and runs locally on two Mac Studios with 512 GB of unified memory each, according to Meta.
Weights are on Hugging Face.

The license is free to use but requires the label "Built with Muse Spark Open." Providers pulling in more than $20 million a year who want to offer the model as an API service need a separate agreement with Meta.
More details are in the research blog.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Sweden is joining European Skills Academies for Quantum and AI, with Nordita supporting the Nordic-Baltic Quantum Academy and Swedish organizations contributing to AI skills development.
The European Quantum Skills Academy (EQA) brings together 73 partners and more than 100 affiliates across 23 countries, with a €19.8 million budget over 48 months and 50% direct EU funding.

The AI Skills Academy initiative in Sweden will focus on AI education for sectors including healthcare and social care, with an emphasis on user participation, democratic principles and responsible technology use.
PRESS RELEASE — As quantum technologies transition from the laboratory to the market, the demand for a highly skilled workforce has never been greater.

Nordita, the Nordic Institute for Theoretical Physics in Stockholm, will play a key role in this initiative supporting the leadership of the Nordic-Baltic Quantum Academy — one of the EQA’s six regional quantum academies.
Supported by a total budget of €19.8 million over 48 months (with 50% of it directly financed by the European Union) the EQA is the largest community in quantum workforce development to date.
The project unites 73 partners and over 100 affiliates spanning 23 European countries.

These efforts align as well with the newly published Swedish strategy for quantum technology, in which Nordic Quantum — a network coordinated from Nordita — is highlighted as an example of collaboration in the Nordic region.
The fact that Sweden via Nordita and Stockholm University enters the newly established European Skills Academy is highly welcome, notes Director General and Sweden’s Science Council Katarina Bjelke.
Now, through the Nordic-Baltic Quantum Academy, Nordita ensures that Sweden and its neighbors remain deeply integrated into the European quantum landscape.

By expanding access to experimental and digital infrastructures, the EQA will serve as Europe’s anchor for quantum skills, ensuring global leadership in a domain critical for future innovation and security.

European AI Skills Academy Sweden, through Region Värmland and Experio Lab in collaboration with researchers affiliated with WASP-HS and other stakeholders, will participate actively in the European Skills Academy for EU.

items.title: AI agents develop their own 'artificial natural language' to communicate about complex data
items.originalTitle: AI agents develop their own 'artificial natural language' to communicate about complex data
items.summary: Jérôme Botoko Ekila, a doctoral student at the VUB's AI Lab, explains, "Instead of forcing AI systems to communicate in a human language that does not correspond to their sensors, we allow them to develop their own 'artificial natural language.' They construct effective concepts that correspond exactly to what they perceive via their sensors, even if the data is incomprehensible to humans." Because sensors on different machines or vehicles can never be calibrated identically in practice, the researchers believe that this language offers the ideal solution.

evidenceRecords.text: Jérôme Botoko Ekila, a doctoral student at the VUB's AI Lab, explains, "Instead of forcing AI systems to communicate in a human language that does not correspond to their sensors, we allow them to develop their own 'artificial natural language.' They construct effective concepts that correspond exactly to what they perceive via their sensors, even if the data is incomprehensible to humans."
Because sensors on different machines or vehicles can never be calibrated identically in practice, the researchers believe that this language offers the ideal solution.

Paul Van Eecke, a professor of artificial intelligence at the VUB, says, "In industrial or physical applications, it is simply unrealistic to expect all the sensors on different robots or vehicles to be calibrated in exactly the same way.
"Humans solve this problem through language: if I say I am standing near the 'red car,' we understand each other without our eyes registering exactly the same color values.
Language provides a layer of abstraction above the sensor readings, and this is precisely what we are now allowing these AI agents to construct autonomously."

Instead of preprogrammed words or fixed codes, the researchers provided the agents with the basic mechanisms underpinning the evolution of human language: the local invention of words, the adaptation of conceptual prototypes and the incorporation of feedback following successful or failed communication.
Katrien Beuls, a professor at UNamur, explains, "What's fascinating is that there's no central computer imposing the rules.
Each time, we let two agents communicate with one another at a local level.
It is solely through these individual interactions and updates that a global convention emerges spontaneously across the entire population.
The universal applicability of the method has been demonstrated across 37 varied and complex data sets.
The agents successfully developed their own vocabulary to communicate, notably regarding physicochemical analyses of wine, NASA data on exoplanets, visual data sets and images of birds or faces.
In all these situations, the agents successfully synthesized the data into new, shared concepts.

items.title: Scaling Indic Pretraining: 2.8 Trillion Tokens and an Open Data Generation Pipeline
items.originalTitle: Scaling Indic Pretraining: 2.8 Trillion Tokens and an Open Data Generation Pipeline
items.summary: We're excited to introduce Nemotron-pretraining-Indic-v1 approximately 2.8 trillion tokens across 22 Indian languages, releasing soon alongside the open, GPU-accelerated data generation pipeline used to create it. Developed by NVIDIA with IIT Madras, India's premier engineering institute, and its AI4Bharat lab, this release gives model builders a substantial new resource for Indic pretraining. evidenceRecords.text: We're excited to introduce Nemotron-pretraining-Indic-v1 approximately 2.8 trillion tokens across 22 Indian languages, releasing soon alongside the open, GPU-accelerated data generation pipeline used to create it.
Developed by NVIDIA with IIT Madras, India's premier engineering institute, and its AI4Bharat lab, this release gives model builders a substantial new resource for Indic pretraining.
The pipeline captures the full generation recipe, including prompts, LLM workflows, and quality checks, so developers can adapt it to their own source material and generate more data for their needs.
AI4Bharat, IIT Madras' Indian language research lab, builds open-source datasets and models for Indian languages.
Its resources, such as Sangraha, an open pretraining corpus for 22 Indian languages, have helped lay the foundation for open Indic language-model research.
Our joint open-source release represents a substantial expansion of the open synthetic Indic training data that will be available to the community.

It brings a broad mix of curated English material, including mathematics, code, and question-answer content, into Indian languages, giving teams more training material for building models that can explain technical concepts, work through problems, and answer questions in those languages.
Every record traces back to a curated source document, and each output is checked against its input, so the synthetic text stays grounded in real information.
We're sharing the open generation recipe so the community can not just reproduce the data but take this work further.
Teams can use the corpus directly, adapt the prompts and quality checks, or bring their own source documents to the workflow.
By opening up both the data and the process, we aim to make large-scale Indic data generation more accessible and enable more developers to contribute to stronger models across Indian languages.

The companion reports, [*Scaling Synthetic Pre-training Data and Evaluation for Indic LLMs*](Scaling Synthetic Pre-training Data and Evaluation for Indic LLMs.pdf and the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Lightning technical report, provide the corpus accounting, generation methods, experiments, and evaluation details.

Black Forest Labs says it scores the highest Elo ratings among all open models in internal testing, beating closed competitors Ideogram V4.5 and even BFL's own FLUX.2 [pro]. Founder of the AI-fueled calorie tracking app Cal AI, Yadegari is only 19 but his company has rocketed to viral fame over the past two years.
At TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday, Yadegari shared details of that surprising rise to prominence.
Cal AI, which was founded in 2024, exploded onto the internet thanks largely to Yadegari’s strategy of deploying a small army of influencers to promote the brand.
The company generated over $30 million in revenue in two years and was acquired by MyFitnessPal for an undisclosed amount of money in March.
Discussing his social strategy onstage, Yadegari noted that an early sign of success came when an influencer’s post about them led to approximately a thousand new users over the course of two days.
The Forbes 30 Under 30 alumnus told the audience that part of his company’s strategy was to negotiate rates with influencers, promising them certain payouts for a certain scale of reach.

A lot of influencers are “broke college kids” who “just want cash,” Yadegari added. “You just ask them, okay, we’ll pay you this, but we need to get us at least this amount of use and keep posting until you get there.”

Another important component of success was finding the right influencers whose reach can be quantified. “The biggest thing for us was finding influencers that had very tight communities,” the founder said.
Yadegari, whose father was in the audience, also credited his family with giving him the freedom to go after his ambitions.
Does he also credit higher education for his success?

items.summary: Anthropic is giving employee-level access to six researchers from METR, a nonprofit that tests frontier AI models, to independently assess Anthropic’s models, safety practices, and risk management, the company said in a blog post on Thursday. “We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making,” Anthropic said in the blog post.

evidenceRecords.text: Anthropic is giving employee-level access to six researchers from METR, a nonprofit that tests frontier AI models, to independently assess Anthropic’s models, safety practices, and risk management, the company said in a blog post on Thursday.

“We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making,” Anthropic said in the blog post. “We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.”

Under the new arrangement, the METR team has Anthropic-issued company laptops, office space, and access to internal tools roughly on par with what Anthropic’s own risk assessment teams use. “Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk” the company said.
Anthropic compared the arrangement to banking, similar to how regulators place resident examiners inside the largest banks.
METR will publish its own assessments of Anthropic’s risks, incidents, and practices, and the company has given up the right to block them.

“Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into narrow, pre-defined categories,” the company said, such as customer data, anything attorney-client privileged, or relating to information about its model architectures. “METR is free to characterize our redactions publicly, and say whether it believes the redactions were justified, as long as it does so without revealing the redacted information” Anthropic added.
METR is the only evaluator so far at the top of a three-tier system Anthropic is building.
Evaluators in the bottom tier, like biosecurity nonprofit SecureBio, run narrow reviews and require Anthropic’s approval to publish.
The middle tier gets more information and can publish without approval, while the top tier adds METR’s employee-level access.

Thursday’s announcement makes good on a promise Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei made in a September essay, where he proposed embedding outside evaluators inside AI labs as a first step toward slowing the technology’s development.

CMR Surgical gets clearance for more procedures CMR Surgical said that Versius can help healthcare providers grow robotic adoption within existing operating room workflows.
This scalable approach can help health systems meet growing demand for robotic-assisted surgery while preserving operational flexibility and supporting long-term program economics, added the company.

“We selected CMR Surgical and the Versius portfolio because of the opportunity to help healthcare providers grow robotic-assisted surgery adoption across a broad range of procedures in hospitals and ASCs.” “We also look forward to welcoming Andy Pierce to our board of directors and benefiting from his more than 30 years of MedTech leadership experience at Stryker as we continue expanding access to robotic-assisted surgery globally,” said Colella.

Moving forward, Stryker will serve as the exclusive U.S. sales agent for the Versius portfolio, while CMR Surgical will continue to lead portfolio development and commercialization in markets outside the United States.
Stryker’s exclusive acquisition option gives it the option of buying 100% of CMR Surgical’s outstanding equity in the future, subject to the agreement’s terms.

items.summary: This episode of the Physics World Weekly podcast features Ignacio Cirac , who has won the 2026 Isaac Newton Medal and Lecture for his “pioneering contributions that founded modern quantum information science, uniting profound theoretical insight, experimental vision, and exceptional scientific leadership shaping quantum physics and technology worldwide”. Cirac is director of the theory division at the Max-Planck-Institute for Quantum Optics in Germany.

evidenceRecords.text: This episode of the Physics World Weekly podcast features Ignacio Cirac , who has won the 2026 Isaac Newton Medal and Lecture for his “pioneering contributions that founded modern quantum information science, uniting profound theoretical insight, experimental vision, and exceptional scientific leadership shaping quantum physics and technology worldwide”.
Cirac is director of the theory division at the Max-Planck-Institute for Quantum Optics in Germany.

In conversation with Physics World ’s Michael Banks, Cirac explains how an early interest in mathematics and science fiction drew him to quantum information – along with the field’s potential to create new technologies.
Cirac weighs up the pros and cons of the qubit technologies available today and highlights the benefits of systems based on Rydberg atoms.
Looking to the future, Cirac cautions against quantum hype and points out that it is still not clear how quantum technologies will be used in the future.
He also calls on European academics to maintain their scientific excellence and for more money to be invested in the continent’s quantum industries.
